Sorry for the long post, I just figured it would be better to have it all in one rather than clutter the group. Thanks for any help!

I don't think time-varying detector covariates are ever going to work, but there is a workaround where you treat each detector x time as a different detector, and switch them on and off via usage. Maybe start with 'secr' rather than 'openCR' - fewer things to get your head around.
Murray

messages.subject: secrdesign 2.5.7 bug in D-hat and RB(D-hat) when using openCR.fit with nrepeats>1
messages.subject_clean: secrdesign 2.5.7 bug in D-hat and RB(D-hat) when using openCR.fit with nrepeats>1
messages.body_plain:
Since version 2.5.5 (Dec 2018) secrdesign has allowed a choice between secr.fit and openCR.fit (openCR package) in simulations for closed population models (run.scenarios or optimalSpacing). openCR.fit is much faster. However, I overlooked that predict.openCR ignores nrepeats>1 (specifically, predict.openCR does not divide the estimated density by nrepeats as it should). As a result, simulated density estimates are high by a factor of nrepeats, and true RB(D-hat) = (RB+1)/nrepeats - 1. RSE(D-hat) is unaffected.

This will be fixed, or an error flag raised, in secrdesign 2.5.8, probably out in March.

messages.subject: Re: OpenCR fiiting problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ujjwal

It's true that openCR.fit does not implement the 'hybrid mixture models' that allow you to include missing values for sex in secr.fit. That may be the whole of your problem - I don't know.

In general, I warn that openCR is not supported to the same level as secr, as I warned somewhere in the documentation. I would not be trying to fit a movement model or sex model, or even a spatial model, until everything else is sorted.

Cheers
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hello, as the subject suggests, I am hoping to get confidence intervals around session-specific population estimates output from the "derived" function used on a openCR.fit model object.

I attempted to follow the workaround suggested by Dr. Efford in the vignette, which reads as follows: "(i) infer the point estimates with derived, (ii) assemble a start vector on the link scale(s) for an equivalent full-likelihood openCR.fit model that includes the derived abundances, and (iii) run openCR.fit with method = "none" to compute the hessian at the MLE, and hence the full variance-covariance matrix."

I can get to the last step, but I only see a superN parameter in the model results. I imagine I need to do something to get from this superN variance-covariance matrix to compute session-specific CIs, but lack the experience to know what this is. Also, the CIs I was hoping to compute are around session-specific population size estimates that were computed with the "HTbysession=TRUE" option in the "derived" function. Does this change the necessary steps to get CIs?

Thanks very much for any insight anyone can grant me. I can post code and/or data if needed.

Best,
Thomas

Murray

messages.subject: Re: OpenCR fiiting problem
messages.body_plain:
One thing I always forget to mention when directing someone to the Bayesian-based package is that they might need to run 20 chains or so to get an acceptable effective sample size for the dispersal sigma, so maybe I'm the one flirting with computational intractability! You can do them in parallel, though, if you have the resources. I haven't run into multimodality with unknown sexes, yet. I understand how this happens with completely latent finite mixtures, but don't see how it happens when they are partially observed and so there is no label switching.

Of the 3 data sets I've explored with the package so far, they've all had interesting sex-specific population dynamics and/or dispersal differences.

I take that back, with large sex differences in sigma, I've seen some multimodality in the sex-specific sigma as influential unknown sex individuals are updated from male to female and vice versa. I haven't seen this propagate to other parameters we care more about, though. This is fine except it complicates the decision about how to calculate the point estimate for sigma (posterior mode, mean, median, etc.)

messages.subject: Re: OpenCR fiiting problem
messages.body_plain:
One other distinction between how sex is handled in openCR and OpenPopSCR may be the population growth model. Does openCR allow covariates on per capita recruitment? If so, what is the implied population growth model when that covariate is sex?

In OpenPopSCR, gamma^m and gamma^f are the per sex per capita recruitment rates--how many males per N and females per N are added to the population each year.  N^m_t= N^m_{t-1}*(phi^m+gamma^m) and N^f_t= N^f_{t-1}*(phi^f+gamma^f) with N^total_t= N^m_t +N^f_t. So you can estimate sex by year N and D, yearly sex ratio, and sex-specific and total population growth rate by inter-primary period.
